vo.text: In 1260, the Mongols had conquered more land than anyone in history. Their armies almost never lost. Then they rode into Palestine, and met an army that knew a trick or two.
The Mongol Empire stretched from China to Eastern Europe. Two years earlier, they had destroyed Baghdad. Now they had taken Damascus.
Their leader, Hulagu, sent a message to Egypt: surrender, or else. The rulers of Egypt, the Mamluks, sent back their answer. It was not polite. Let's leave it at that.
Then luck changed. Far away in Mongolia, the Great Khan died, and Hulagu took most of his army back east. He left a smaller army behind, under a general named Kitbuqa.
The Mamluk sultan Qutuz marched out with his toughest general, Baybars.
On the third of September, 1260, they met the Mongols near a spring called Ain Jalut, Goliath's Spring, in a valley below the hills of Galilee.
And the Mamluks used one of the Mongols' favourite tricks against them.
Baybars rode out with a small force, fought for a while, and then pretended to run away. Up the valley.
The Mongols, who loved this trick themselves, charged straight after him.
Hidden in the hills, the main Mamluk army was waiting.
Ambush. The Mongols were hit from the sides.
The Mongols fought back hard, and for a moment the Mamluk line began to bend. Qutuz threw his helmet to the ground and shouted: Oh Islam! And his men rallied.
The Mamluks charged again. Kitbuqa was killed, and the Mongol army was broken.
The Mongols, who almost never lost, had been beaten. And this time they could not come back for revenge. They never conquered Egypt.
As for Qutuz: on the way home, Baybars got rid of him, and made himself sultan. Teamwork.
The Mamluks went on to rule Egypt for more than two hundred and fifty years.
